nameStory: Intermediate cinquefoil gets its name from the French 'cinq-feuille' meaning 'five leaves,' referring to the typical five-leaflet pattern of most cinquefoils. The 'intermediate' part of its name reflects its position between other cinquefoil species in botanical classification, sharing characteristics with multiple relatives.
description: Intermediate cinquefoil is a low-growing perennial herb in the rose family that produces small yellow flowers with five rounded petals. This European native typically grows 6-12 inches tall with a spreading habit. Like other cinquefoils, it has compound leaves divided into several leaflets and belongs to the same family as roses and strawberries. It's extremely rare in New England, with only a couple recorded sightings.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Bright yellow flowers with five rounded petals that feel papery when touched, about half an inch across, blooming from late spring through summer

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Compound leaves typically divided into 5-7 toothed leaflets that feel slightly rough and hairy to the touch, arranged in a palmate pattern like fingers on a hand

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Low, spreading perennial that forms mats or patches, rarely exceeding one foot in height with stems that may root where they touch the ground

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Small, dry fruits clustered together in the center where the flower was, turning brown and papery as they mature

habitat: In its native range, intermediate cinquefoil grows in disturbed soils, roadsides, and waste areas. The few New England records suggest it appears in similar disturbed habitats, likely as an occasional introduction rather than an established population.

seasonality.spring: New leaves emerge and plants begin active growth, with early flowers appearing by late spring on established plants.
seasonality.summer: Peak flowering period with bright yellow blooms most visible, and leaves at their fullest development.
seasonality.fall: Flowers fade and seed heads mature, while leaves may begin to yellow and die back in preparation for winter.
seasonality.winter: Plants die back to ground level in cold climates, surviving as underground rootstock until spring returns.

funFact: Despite being called 'intermediate' cinquefoil, this species has traveled an incredible distance from its native range spanning from Poland all the way to the Russian Far East, making its rare appearances in New England quite the botanical surprise!
confusionNotes: With only two recorded observations in New England, intermediate cinquefoil is most likely to be confused with the much more common sulphur cinquefoil or common cinquefoil. Look for the specific leaflet arrangement and compare with local field guides, as proper identification of this rarity is crucial for botanical records.
contextualKnowledge: As an extremely rare species in New England with only two recorded observations, any sighting of intermediate cinquefoil should be photographed and reported to local botanists or naturalist organizations, as it may represent new introductions or overlooked populations.
compareHints: Intermediate cinquefoil differs from common New England cinquefoils like dwarf cinquefoil by its specific leaflet count and arrangement, and from sulphur cinquefoil by its smaller stature and different leaf texture. Unlike the native common cinquefoil which spreads by runners, intermediate cinquefoil has a more clumping growth pattern.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Sulphur cinquefoil stands out from other New England cinquefoils primarily by its bright yellow flowers and consistently five-fingered leaves.

Among New England's cinquefoils, silvery cinquefoil is the only one with dramatically silver-white fuzzy leaf undersides - dwarf and common cinquefoil have plain green undersides, while rough cinquefoil has much larger, coarsely-toothed leaves.
Among New England's cinquefoils, dwarf cinquefoil is distinguished by its truly prostrate, mat-forming habit with rooting runners.
Common cinquefoil differs from dwarf cinquefoil by its longer, more obvious runners and slightly larger flowers.
Unlike other cinquefoils in its genus which typically have five-part leaves (the name cinquefoil means 'five leaves'), mock strawberry has three-part leaves like true strawberries.
Unlike most other New England cinquefoils which have five leaflets, rough cinquefoil stands out with just three leaflets per leaf.
Lesser mock-strawberry differs from other cinquefoils by having three-part leaves instead of the typical five-part leaves (cinque means five in French).
Unlike its lowland cinquefoil relatives that spread by runners or grow as larger plants, dwarf mountain cinquefoil forms tiny, tight cushions and never leaves the alpine zone.

Among New England's cinquefoils, creeping cinquefoil is unique for its long trailing runners and five-leaflet leaves – most other cinquefoils like common cinquefoil and dwarf cinquefoil have three leaflets and don't spread by runners.
Unlike its inland cinquefoil relatives, coast cinquefoil has adapted specifically to maritime conditions with its more compact, mat-forming growth and thicker, more succulent-like leaves.
